title: Mixed sessions, the city ordinance and the union
summary: Interracial sessions risked a city problem and union fines for non-union players; union reps waited outside locked-door sessions.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Talking about, did you have any problems with mixed sessions when they were black-white?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah. I had two problems. I had a city problem.
Yeah, tell me about that. Well, yeah, it was against the law.
But thankfully, nobody ever really made an issue of it. Although some people would mention it, you know.
And the other was, strangely enough, part of the problem was the union.

Not that it was white union, black union guys playing, but that there'd be non-union guys playing with union guys. Oh, you know, all mixed up. And so it was a double problem, you know. I mean, a lot of, a lot, a lot, a lot of, yeah. Yeah. And it worked both ways. We'd have a mixed band, and it'd be some rock and roll kid playing, white or black. He wasn't a union member. You know. And they frowned on that. They really frowned on that. If they got caught, everybody got fined.
For having, for it being mixed or because they were non-union? Non-union. Yeah.

But it got the most attention when it was also mixed for some reason. Or it seemed that way. And I would, you know, I can't point to anybody and say that's the way they looked at it. But it sure seemed that way.
So would, would, would, would there be a union guy come down every night to check?

Well, you know, the agreement, the agreement is that, that the, that the, quote, representative of the laborers has, have access to the place of employment. In other words, if you had a union ban, the, the representative of the union had to be allowed in and on the premises and that kind of stuff. So whenever we had locked door sessions, they'd be waiting outside.
And they'd want to come in.
Yeah. Well, you know, nobody would let them in.
Let them in.
I mean, but, but they could wait outside. And on a few occasions, they actually wrote down all the license plate numbers of the cars in the neighborhood and stuff like that.
Oh, yeah.
Well, generally they couldn't wait that long because the sessions went off for six and eight hours. So they wouldn't, they wouldn't hang around. Although I suppose once or twice they did.
But getting, getting back to the city ordinance, I thought the city ordinance just stated public performance.

Yeah. Well, that was, that was part of the hour. Was that we weren't, yeah, we weren't charged. Right. But, but there were some people who would like to have interpreted it that way. I, I, I can remember a certain civil sheriff, for instance. He was a deputy civil sheriff. He wasn't the civil sheriff. He was a deputy civil sheriff. And he was a racist SOB. And he said something to me one day about mixed sessions. Because I ran into him on another, on another basis. And, and I told him, I said, well, you know, that's, that's not, not, not public performance and all that.
And he said, well, he said, well, he probably lucky it isn't something to that effect.
But there weren't a lot of people that would be that militant about it. But some people took offense.
Yeah. I mean, who, who, who, who. Who cared?
Most people didn't even know about it.
Yeah. Most people didn't even know. Who cared? Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. That's, that was, that was a lot we had. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And then, and then getting back, today we, we open up Friday and get the, you know, the, But you've got to remember how the paper, for instance, worked.
